name: AP Chemistry
blurb: Nine units, from the mole to the cell

cards.q: Define the mole and state Avogadro's number.
cards.a: A mole is the amount of substance containing 6.022 x 10^23 elementary particles (Avogadro's number, N_A). It is a counting unit, like a dozen.
cards.n: The mole links the particulate world to lab-measurable mass; AP expects it named as a COUNT, not a mass.

cards.q: State the equation relating moles, mass, and molar mass.
cards.a: n = m / M, where n = moles (mol), m = mass (g), and M = molar mass (g/mol).
cards.n: On the AP equations sheet. Units are the fastest check: g ÷ (g/mol) = mol.

cards.q: Define molar mass and give its units.
cards.a: Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol. It is found by summing the atomic masses (from the periodic table) of every atom in the formula.

cards.q: Compute the number of molecules in 36.0 g of H₂O.
cards.a: M(H₂O) = 18.0 g/mol, so n = 36.0/18.0 = 2.00 mol. Particles = 2.00 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 1.20 x 10^24 molecules.
cards.n: Trap: for atoms rather than molecules you must multiply again by atoms per formula unit (here x3).

cards.q: Explain how to read a mass spectrum of a pure element.
cards.a: Each peak is one isotope. The horizontal axis is mass/charge (m/z), which for a 1+ ion equals the isotope's mass number. Peak height gives the relative natural abundance of that isotope.
cards.h: → what each axis and each peak means

cards.q: Compute average atomic mass from isotopic masses and abundances.
cards.a: Average atomic mass = Σ (isotope mass x fractional abundance). Example: 75.0% ³⁵Cl (34.97) + 25.0% ³⁷Cl (36.97) gives 0.750(34.97) + 0.250(36.97) = 35.5 amu.
cards.n: Trap: convert percentages to decimals; abundances must sum to 1. Do NOT take a simple average of the isotope masses.

cards.q: Explain why an element's average atomic mass lies closer to the mass of one particular isotope.
cards.a: The average is weighted by abundance, so it is pulled toward whichever isotope is most abundant. Cl averages 35.45 because ³⁵Cl is about three times as common as ³⁷Cl.
cards.n: Useful check: if your computed average is not between the lightest and heaviest isotope mass, you made an arithmetic error.

cards.q: Define percent composition by mass and give the equation.
cards.a: Percent composition is the mass fraction of each element in a compound: %element = (mass of that element in 1 mol / molar mass of compound) x 100%.
cards.n: Percent composition is identical for every sample of a pure compound - this is the law of definite proportions.

cards.q: Contrast an empirical formula with a molecular formula.
cards.a: The empirical formula is the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms (CH₂O). The molecular formula gives the actual atom counts in one molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) and is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
cards.n: Percent composition data alone can NEVER give a molecular formula; you also need the molar mass.

cards.q: Apply the standard procedure for finding an empirical formula from percent composition.
cards.a: 1) Assume 100 g, so percents become grams. 2) Divide each mass by that element's molar mass to get moles. 3) Divide all mole values by the smallest. 4) Multiply to clear fractions to whole numbers.
cards.n: Trap: a ratio like 1:1.5 must be doubled to 2:3, not rounded to 1:2.

cards.q: Compute a molecular formula given an empirical formula and molar mass.
cards.a: Find n = (molar mass of compound) / (empirical formula mass), then multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n. If CH₂O (30.0) and M = 180 g/mol, n = 6, so the formula is C₆H₁₂O₆.

cards.q: Contrast a pure substance with a mixture.
cards.a: A pure substance has fixed composition and identical particles throughout, so it has sharp, characteristic physical properties. A mixture contains two or more substances in variable proportion and is separated by physical means that exploit property differences.

cards.q: Explain the physical property that filtration exploits.
cards.a: Filtration separates by particle size: an insoluble solid is trapped by the filter while the solution or liquid passes through. It works only when one component is not dissolved.
cards.n: Trap: filtration cannot separate a dissolved solute from its solvent - the ions pass through the paper.

cards.q: Explain the physical property that distillation exploits.
cards.a: Distillation separates by boiling point, which is set by intermolecular force strength. The component with the weaker IMFs (lower boiling point) vaporizes first, is condensed, and is collected separately.

cards.q: Explain the principle behind chromatographic separation.
cards.a: Components distribute between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. A component with stronger attraction to the mobile phase (and weaker attraction to the stationary phase) travels farther; stronger stationary-phase attraction means it lags behind.

cards.q: State Coulomb's law as it is used to explain atomic and ionic attractions.
cards.a: The magnitude of the potential energy between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges divided by the distance between them: E ∝ q₁q₂ / r (the force follows an inverse-square law, F ∝ q₁q₂ / r²). Opposite charges give negative (attractive) energy.
cards.n: Nearly every 'why' question about radius, ionization energy, and lattice energy is answered with charge and distance.

cards.q: Define effective nuclear charge and shielding.
cards.a: Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) is the net positive charge an electron actually experiences. Inner-shell (core) electrons repel outer electrons and shield them from the nucleus, so Z_eff is less than the full nuclear charge.

cards.q: State the maximum number of electrons in the s, p, d, and f subshells.
cards.a: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14. Shell n holds up to 2n² electrons total.

cards.q: State the three rules that govern the order of filling atomic orbitals.
cards.a: Aufbau: fill lowest-energy orbitals first. Pauli exclusion: max two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins. Hund's rule: within a degenerate subshell, place one electron in each orbital before pairing.

cards.q: Recall the two anomalous electron configurations expected on the AP exam.
cards.a: Cr is [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ and Cu is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, not 4s²3d⁴ / 4s²3d⁹. A half-filled or completely filled d subshell is lower in energy.
cards.n: Mo and Ag follow the same pattern. AP asks for these mainly in PES and ionization-energy contexts.

cards.q: State the rule for writing the electron configuration of a transition metal cation.
cards.a: Write the neutral atom's configuration, then remove electrons from the highest n shell first - that is, remove the s electrons before any d electrons. Fe ([Ar]4s²3d⁶) becomes Fe³⁺ = [Ar]3d⁵.
cards.n: Classic trap: students remove 3d before 4s. Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶, NOT [Ar]4s²3d⁴.

cards.q: Explain what a photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) spectrum measures and how its axes are arranged.
cards.a: PES measures the binding energy needed to eject electrons from each subshell. The x-axis is binding energy, conventionally increasing to the LEFT, so core electrons appear on the left and valence electrons on the right. Each peak is one subshell.
cards.n: Trap: the axis runs backwards. The leftmost peak is 1s (highest binding energy), not the outermost electrons.

cards.q: Identify what the height (relative intensity) of a PES peak tells you.
cards.a: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell. A 1s peak of relative height 2 and a 2p peak of height 4 means 2 electrons in 1s and 4 in 2p.

cards.q: Apply PES data to identify an element: peaks at 126, 9.07, 5.31, and 0.74 MJ/mol with relative heights 2, 2, 6, 2.
cards.a: The heights give 1s²2s²2p⁶3s², which totals 12 electrons, so the element is magnesium.

cards.q: Explain why the 2s peak appears at higher binding energy than the 2p peak in the same atom.
cards.a: 2s electrons penetrate closer to the nucleus than 2p electrons, so they experience a larger effective nuclear charge and are held more tightly, requiring more energy to remove.

cards.q: Explain the periodic trend in atomic radius and its cause.
cards.a: Radius decreases left to right across a period because Z_eff rises while electrons are added to the same shell, pulling the shell inward. Radius increases down a group because electrons occupy shells of higher n, farther from the nucleus, with more shielding.
cards.h: → two directions, each with a reason

cards.q: Contrast the size of a cation and an anion with the neutral parent atom.
cards.a: A cation is smaller than its parent atom: fewer electrons means less repulsion and a larger Z_eff per electron (often a whole shell is lost). An anion is larger: added electrons increase electron-electron repulsion while nuclear charge is unchanged.

cards.q: Rank the isoelectronic ions N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, and Mg²⁺ by radius, largest first.
cards.a: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺. All have 10 electrons, so the one with the largest nuclear charge (most protons) pulls them in tightest.
cards.n: Isoelectronic series are ranked ONLY by proton count; never by position in the periodic table.

cards.q: Explain the periodic trend in first ionization energy and its cause.
cards.a: First ionization energy increases across a period (higher Z_eff holds valence electrons more tightly) and decreases down a group (the valence electron is farther out and better shielded, so Coulombic attraction is weaker).
cards.h: → two directions, each with a reason

cards.q: Identify the two places where first ionization energy dips against the general trend.
cards.a: Group 2 to 13 (Be > B): boron's electron comes from a higher-energy 2p orbital. Group 15 to 16 (N > O): oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair in an already-occupied orbital, and the added repulsion makes it easier to remove.
cards.h: → two group pairs + a reason each
cards.n: These dips are prime FRQ material because they force you to argue from subshell energy and electron pairing, not just Z_eff.

cards.q: Explain what a large jump between successive ionization energies reveals.
cards.a: A large jump occurs when the next electron must come from a lower, core shell. The number of electrons removed BEFORE the jump equals the number of valence electrons, which identifies the element's group.
cards.h: → what the jump marks + what you can count
cards.n: AP loves giving a table of IE₁...IE₅ and asking for the group. Count the small values before the big gap.

cards.q: Define electronegativity and state its periodic trend.
cards.a: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract the shared electrons in a bond toward itself. It increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
cards.n: Trap: electronegativity applies to atoms IN a bond; ionization energy and electron affinity apply to isolated gaseous atoms.

cards.q: Define electron affinity and state how it varies across a period.
cards.a: Electron affinity is the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron. It becomes more negative (more energy released) across a period as Z_eff increases; halogens have the most negative values, noble gases essentially none.

cards.q: Identify the number of valence electrons for main-group elements from the periodic table.
cards.a: For groups 1, 2, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 the valence electron counts are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 respectively. Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell (highest n).
cards.h: → mapping of group to a number

cards.q: Predict the ion charge formed by each main group: 1, 2, 13, 15, 16, 17.
cards.a: Group 1 forms 1+, group 2 forms 2+, group 13 forms 3+, group 15 forms 3-, group 16 forms 2-, group 17 forms 1-. Each atom gains or loses electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration.

cards.q: Explain why metals form cations and nonmetals form anions.
cards.a: Metals have low ionization energies, so their valence electrons are removed easily. Nonmetals have high Z_eff and very negative electron affinities, so gaining electrons is energetically favorable and completes their valence shell.
cards.h: → IE for one, EA for the other

cards.q: Name and give the formulas of the nitrogen oxyanions.
cards.a: Nitrate is NO₃⁻ and nitrite is NO₂⁻. Both carry a 1- charge; -ate has one more oxygen than -ite.

cards.q: Name and give the formulas of the sulfur oxyanions.
cards.a: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻ and sulfite is SO₃²⁻. Both carry a 2- charge.

cards.q: Recall the formulas and charges of phosphate and ammonium.
cards.a: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻ (3-) and ammonium is NH₄⁺ (1+). Ammonium is the only common polyatomic CATION on the AP exam.

cards.q: Recall the formulas and charges of carbonate and bicarbonate.
cards.a: Carbonate is CO₃²⁻ (2-) and bicarbonate, also called hydrogen carbonate, is HCO₃⁻ (1-). Adding H⁺ to a polyatomic ion raises its charge by one.

cards.q: Recall the formulas of hydroxide, cyanide, and peroxide.
cards.a: Hydroxide is OH⁻, cyanide is CN⁻, and peroxide is O₂²⁻. In peroxide each oxygen has oxidation number -1 rather than the usual -2.

cards.q: Recall the formula of the acetate ion.
cards.a: Acetate is CH₃COO⁻, also written C₂H₃O₂⁻, with a 1- charge. It is the conjugate base of acetic acid, CH₃COOH.

cards.q: Recall the formulas and charges of chromate, dichromate, and permanganate.
cards.a: Chromate is CrO₄²⁻ (2-), dichromate is Cr₂O₇²⁻ (2-), and permanganate is MnO₄⁻ (1-). All three are strong oxidizing agents.

cards.q: State the naming pattern for the four chlorine oxyanions and give their formulas.
cards.a: Hypochlorite ClO⁻, chlorite ClO₂⁻, chlorate ClO₃⁻, perchlorate ClO₄⁻ - all 1-. The pattern is hypo--ite (one less O than -ite), -ite, -ate, per--ate (one more O than -ate).
cards.h: → four names in order + the prefix rule
cards.n: The same hypo-/per- pattern works for bromine and iodine oxyanions; only the oxygen count changes.

cards.q: Contrast ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding in terms of what happens to valence electrons.
cards.a: Ionic: electrons are transferred from metal to nonmetal, and the resulting cations and anions attract electrostatically. Covalent: electrons are shared between two nonmetals. Metallic: valence electrons are delocalized over a lattice of metal cations.
cards.h: → three bond types, one clause each

cards.q: Predict bond type from an electronegativity difference (ΔEN).
cards.a: ΔEN below about 0.4 gives a nonpolar covalent bond; roughly 0.4 to 1.7 gives a polar covalent bond; above about 1.7 gives an ionic bond. Metal + nonmetal is the quick check for ionic.
cards.n: AP prefers reasoning from position in the periodic table over memorized cut-offs; treat the numbers as a guide, not a law.

cards.q: Contrast a polar covalent bond with a nonpolar covalent bond.
cards.a: In a polar covalent bond the atoms have different electronegativities, so the shared electron density sits closer to the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges (δ+ / δ-). In a nonpolar bond the electronegativities are equal or nearly equal and sharing is even.

cards.q: Explain what the minimum of a potential energy versus internuclear distance curve represents.
cards.a: The minimum occurs at the equilibrium bond length, where attraction between each nucleus and the shared electrons exactly balances nuclear-nuclear and electron-electron repulsion. The depth of the well below zero is the bond energy.
cards.n: Trap: at distances shorter than the minimum the energy rises steeply because of nucleus-nucleus repulsion, not because the bond weakens.

cards.q: State how bond order, bond length, and bond strength are related.
cards.a: Higher bond order means a shorter bond and a stronger bond (larger bond energy). C-C > C=C > C≡C in length; C≡C > C=C > C-C in strength.

cards.q: Explain why breaking a chemical bond always requires energy input.
cards.a: The bonded state is lower in potential energy than the separated atoms, so energy must be added to climb out of the potential energy well. Bond breaking is always endothermic; bond forming is always exothermic.

cards.q: Define lattice energy and list the two factors that control its magnitude.
cards.a: Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions combine into one mole of an ionic solid (or the energy needed to separate it). By Coulomb's law it increases with larger ion charges and with smaller ionic radii.

cards.q: Rank the lattice energies of NaCl, MgO, and KCl and justify the order.
cards.a: MgO > NaCl > KCl. MgO has 2+/2- charges rather than 1+/1-, which dominates. NaCl beats KCl because Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺, giving a shorter interionic distance.
cards.n: Charge always outweighs size on the AP exam; compare charges first, then radii only as a tiebreaker.

cards.q: Explain why ionic solids are hard but brittle.
cards.a: The lattice of alternating charges is held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions, so it is hard. When a layer is displaced, like charges align, and the sudden repulsion splits the crystal along that plane.

cards.q: Explain why an ionic compound conducts electricity when molten or dissolved but not as a solid.
cards.a: Conduction requires mobile charge carriers. In the solid, ions are locked in fixed lattice positions; melting or dissolving frees the ions to move and carry current.

cards.q: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
cards.a: Melting requires overcoming strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions throughout a three-dimensional lattice. Because these Coulombic forces are far stronger than intermolecular forces, a large amount of thermal energy is needed.

cards.q: Explain metallic bonding using the sea-of-electrons model and use it to account for two metal properties.
cards.a: Metal atoms release valence electrons into a delocalized 'sea' surrounding a lattice of cations. The mobile electrons carry charge and heat (conductivity), and because the bonding is nondirectional the cations can slide past one another without breaking bonds (malleability and ductility).

cards.q: Contrast a substitutional alloy with an interstitial alloy.
cards.a: In a substitutional alloy, atoms of similar radius replace host atoms in the lattice (brass: Zn in Cu). In an interstitial alloy, much smaller atoms fit into the holes between host atoms (steel: C in Fe).

cards.q: Explain why alloys are generally harder and less malleable than the pure metal.
cards.a: Atoms of a different size disrupt the regular lattice, so layers of atoms can no longer slide smoothly past one another. Interstitial atoms also lock the lattice in place, which raises hardness and strength.

cards.q: State the procedure for drawing a Lewis structure.
cards.a: 1) Total the valence electrons, adjusting for overall charge. 2) Place the least electronegative atom (never H) in the center and connect with single bonds. 3) Complete octets on outer atoms. 4) Put leftovers on the central atom. 5) Form double or triple bonds if the central atom is short of an octet.

cards.q: Apply valence-electron counting to draw the Lewis structure of a polyatomic ion such as SO₄²⁻.
cards.a: Sum the group valence electrons (S = 6, four O = 24, total 30), then ADD one electron for each unit of negative charge (30 + 2 = 32) or subtract for positive charge. Distribute those 32 electrons, then enclose the structure in brackets with the charge outside.
cards.n: Trap: adding electrons for a cation instead of subtracting. NH₄⁺ has 5 + 4 - 1 = 8 valence electrons.

cards.q: Identify the common exceptions to the octet rule.
cards.a: H holds 2 electrons; Be is stable with 4 and B with 6 (electron deficient); elements in period 3 and below (P, S, Cl, Xe) can hold more than 8 by using d orbitals (expanded octet). Odd-electron species such as NO also cannot obey it.

cards.q: State the formula for formal charge.
cards.a: Formal charge = (valence electrons) - (nonbonding electrons) - ½(bonding electrons). Equivalently, valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus number of bonds.

cards.q: Apply formal charge to decide which of several valid Lewis structures is preferred.
cards.a: The best structure has formal charges closest to zero, has no like charges on adjacent atoms, and places any negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom. The sum of formal charges must equal the overall charge.

cards.q: Define resonance and explain what the true structure is.
cards.a: Resonance occurs when more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn by moving only electrons, not atoms. The real molecule is a single averaged hybrid of all contributors, not a mixture that flips between them.
cards.h: → definition + nature of the real species
cards.n: Trap: the molecule does not oscillate between structures. Use a double-headed arrow, never an equilibrium arrow.

cards.q: Predict the bond lengths in the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻.
cards.a: All three C-O bonds are identical and intermediate between a single and a double bond, because the three resonance structures average to a bond order of 4/3 on each bond.

cards.q: Explain why a molecule with resonance is more stable than any single contributing structure.
cards.a: The electrons in the pi system are delocalized over several atoms rather than confined between two. Spreading electron density over a larger volume lowers the potential energy of the molecule, an effect called resonance stabilization.

cards.q: State the central principle of VSEPR theory.
cards.a: Electron domains around a central atom (bonding groups plus lone pairs) repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible, which sets the molecular geometry. A single, double, or triple bond each counts as one domain.

cards.q: Contrast electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry.
cards.a: Electron-domain (electron-pair) geometry counts ALL domains, including lone pairs. Molecular geometry describes the positions of the ATOMS only. NH₃ has tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.
cards.n: Read the question wording carefully: 'shape of the molecule' means molecular geometry, so lone pairs are invisible in the name.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for a central atom with 2 electron domains and no lone pairs.
cards.a: Linear, with a 180° bond angle. Examples: CO₂, BeCl₂, HCN.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 3 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Trigonal planar, with 120° bond angles. Examples: BF₃, SO₃, CO₃²⁻.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 3 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Bent (angular), with a bond angle slightly less than 120° (about 118°). Examples: SO₂, O₃, NO₂⁻.
cards.h: → shape name + angle relative to ideal

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 4 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Tetrahedral, with 109.5° bond angles. Examples: CH₄, NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 4 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Trigonal pyramidal, with bond angles of about 107°, compressed from 109.5° by the lone pair. Example: NH₃.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 4 electron domains with 2 lone pairs.
cards.a: Bent, with a bond angle of about 104.5°. Example: H₂O.
cards.n: Both SO₂ (3 domains) and H₂O (4 domains) are 'bent' but have different angles; state the domain count to justify which.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angles for 5 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Trigonal bipyramidal, with 120° angles in the equatorial plane and 90° between axial and equatorial positions. Example: PCl₅.

cards.q: Predict the geometry for 5 electron domains with 1 lone pair.
cards.a: Seesaw, because the lone pair occupies a roomier equatorial position. Example: SF₄.
cards.h: → shape name + where the lone pair sits

cards.q: Predict the geometries for 5 electron domains with 2 and with 3 lone pairs.
cards.a: Two lone pairs gives T-shaped (ClF₃); three lone pairs gives linear (XeF₂). All lone pairs take equatorial positions.

cards.q: Predict the geometry and bond angle for 6 electron domains with no lone pairs.
cards.a: Octahedral, with 90° bond angles. Example: SF₆.

cards.q: Predict the geometries for 6 electron domains with 1 and with 2 lone pairs.
cards.a: One lone pair gives square pyramidal (BrF₅); two lone pairs gives square planar (XeF₄), with the lone pairs opposite each other at 180°.

cards.q: Explain why lone pairs compress bond angles below the ideal value.
cards.a: A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so its electron cloud is broader and closer to the central atom. It repels bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, pushing the bonds together.

cards.q: Identify the hybridization of a central atom from its number of electron domains.
cards.a: 2 domains = sp, 3 domains = sp², 4 domains = sp³. Lone pairs count as domains, so both H₂O and CH₄ are sp³.
cards.h: → three domain counts mapped to labels
cards.n: Since 2019 the AP CED only requires sp, sp², and sp³; sp³d and sp³d² are no longer assessed.

cards.q: Contrast sigma and pi bonds.
cards.a: A sigma bond forms by head-on (end-to-end) orbital overlap along the internuclear axis and allows free rotation. A pi bond forms by side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below that axis, is weaker, and blocks rotation.

cards.q: Count the sigma and pi bonds in a molecule containing double and triple bonds.
cards.a: Every bond (single, double, or triple) contains exactly one sigma bond. A double bond adds 1 pi bond and a triple bond adds 2 pi bonds. HCN has 2 sigma and 2 pi bonds.

cards.q: Predict whether a molecule is polar from its geometry and bond dipoles.
cards.a: A molecule is polar if the individual bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetric arrangements with identical outer atoms and no lone pairs on the central atom cancel; asymmetry from lone pairs or different outer atoms leaves a net dipole.

cards.q: Identify three molecules that contain polar bonds yet are nonpolar overall.
cards.a: CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), and CCl₄ (tetrahedral). In each, the symmetric arrangement of identical outer atoms makes the bond dipoles cancel to zero.
cards.n: Very common MC distractor: 'has polar bonds' is not the same as 'is a polar molecule'.

cards.q: Rank the intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest.
cards.a: Ion-dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole > dipole-induced dipole > London dispersion (for comparable size). All IMFs are far weaker than ionic, covalent, or metallic bonds.
cards.n: Caveat matters: a very large nonpolar molecule (I₂) can have stronger LDFs than a small polar molecule's dipole-dipole forces.

cards.q: Define London dispersion forces and state which substances have them.
cards.a: LDFs arise from instantaneous, momentary fluctuations in electron distribution that create a temporary dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbor. Every substance has them - they are the only IMF in nonpolar molecules and noble gases.

cards.q: Explain polarizability and how it controls London dispersion strength.
cards.a: Polarizability is how easily an electron cloud is distorted. More electrons (larger molar mass) and a larger, more spread-out cloud mean higher polarizability and stronger LDFs. Long unbranched chains also contact more surface than compact branched isomers.

cards.q: State the requirement for hydrogen bonding.
cards.a: A hydrogen atom must be covalently bonded directly to N, O, or F, and must interact with a lone pair on an N, O, or F of a neighboring molecule. It is an unusually strong dipole-dipole force, not an actual bond.
cards.n: Trap: CH₃OCH₃ has O but no O-H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself, while its isomer CH₃CH₂OH can.

cards.q: Explain the ion-dipole force and name a situation where it dominates.
cards.a: An ion attracts the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule. It is the key force when an ionic solid dissolves in water: Na⁺ is surrounded by the oxygen ends of water molecules and Cl⁻ by the hydrogen ends.

cards.q: Define ion-induced dipole and dipole-induced dipole forces.
cards.a: An ion (or a permanent dipole) distorts the electron cloud of a nearby nonpolar molecule, inducing a temporary dipole that is then attracted to it. These forces explain why O₂ and N₂ dissolve slightly in water.

cards.q: Predict which of two substances has the higher boiling point, and justify it.
cards.a: The substance with stronger intermolecular forces boils higher, because more kinetic energy is needed to separate the particles. Compare IMF type first (H-bonding beats dipole-dipole beats LDF), then molar mass or surface area within the same type.

cards.q: Explain why H₂O, HF, and NH₃ boil far higher than the trend of their families predicts.
cards.a: Each contains H bonded to a highly electronegative small atom (O, F, N), so extensive hydrogen bonding forms. That strong IMF overrides the usual increase in boiling point with molar mass down the group.
cards.h: → named IMF + why it overrides the trend

cards.q: Contrast intermolecular forces with intramolecular forces during boiling.
cards.a: Intramolecular forces are the covalent bonds WITHIN a molecule; intermolecular forces act BETWEEN molecules. Boiling separates molecules from one another, so it overcomes only IMFs - the covalent bonds stay intact.
cards.h: → location of each + which one breaks
cards.n: Very common trap: 'boiling water breaks O-H bonds' is wrong. Water vapor is still H₂O molecules.

cards.q: Explain how IMF strength affects vapor pressure, viscosity, and surface tension.
cards.a: Stronger IMFs mean fewer molecules can escape the liquid, so vapor pressure is LOWER, while resistance to flow (viscosity) and surface tension are HIGHER. Vapor pressure moves opposite to the other two.

cards.q: Contrast the four types of solids by particle, force, melting point, and conductivity.
cards.a: Ionic: ions held by electrostatic attraction, high mp, conducts only when molten or aqueous. Molecular: molecules held by IMFs, low mp, nonconductor. Covalent network: atoms held by covalent bonds, very high mp, nonconductor (except graphite). Metallic: cations in an electron sea, variable mp, conducts as a solid.

cards.q: Identify three covalent network solids and explain their very high melting points.
cards.a: Diamond (C), silicon dioxide (SiO₂), and silicon carbide (SiC). Melting requires breaking a continuous three-dimensional array of strong covalent bonds, not merely overcoming intermolecular forces.

cards.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
cards.a: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others in flat sheets, leaving one delocalized p electron per atom free to move through the layer. In diamond every carbon is sp³ bonded to four neighbors, so all valence electrons are localized in sigma bonds.

cards.q: Predict the type of solid from a data table of melting point and conductivity.
cards.a: High mp + conducts only when molten or aqueous = ionic. Low mp + never conducts = molecular. Very high mp + does not conduct = covalent network. Conducts as a solid and is malleable = metallic.
cards.h: → four property patterns matched to types

cards.q: Identify the six phase changes and state which are endothermic.
cards.a: Melting (fusion), vaporization, and sublimation absorb energy (endothermic). Freezing, condensation, and deposition release energy (exothermic). Each pair is the reverse of the other with an equal magnitude of enthalpy change.
cards.h: → six names sorted by energy sign

cards.q: Identify the axes, the triple point, and the critical point on a phase diagram.
cards.a: The x-axis is temperature and the y-axis is pressure; regions show the stable phase and lines show two phases in equilibrium. The triple point is where all three phases coexist; beyond the critical point liquid and gas become indistinguishable (supercritical fluid).

cards.q: Explain why the solid-liquid boundary on water's phase diagram has a negative slope.
cards.a: Ice is less dense than liquid water because hydrogen bonding holds the molecules in an open lattice. Increasing pressure therefore favors the denser liquid, so the melting point drops as pressure rises - the opposite of nearly every other substance.

cards.q: Define vapor pressure and state the condition for boiling.
cards.a: Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapor in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure.
cards.n: This is why water boils below 100 °C at high altitude: the external pressure is lower.

cards.q: Explain why temperature stays constant during the plateaus of a heating curve.
cards.a: During a phase change all added energy goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions (increasing potential energy) rather than increasing the average kinetic energy of the particles, and temperature measures average kinetic energy only.

cards.q: State the ideal gas law and the value of R.
cards.a: PV = nRT, with R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) or 8.314 J/(mol·K). Temperature must always be in kelvin.
cards.n: Trap: the two R values are not interchangeable. Match R to the pressure units in the problem.

cards.q: State the individual gas relationships contained in the ideal gas law.
cards.a: Boyle: P ∝ 1/V at constant n and T. Charles: V ∝ T at constant n and P. Gay-Lussac: P ∝ T at constant n and V. Avogadro: V ∝ n at constant P and T.

cards.q: Derive an expression for the molar mass of a gas from PV = nRT.
cards.a: Substitute n = m/M into PV = nRT to get PV = (m/M)RT, so M = mRT/(PV). Since density d = m/V, this is equivalently M = dRT/P.

cards.q: Compute the volume occupied by 2.00 mol of an ideal gas at 1.50 atm and 27 °C.
cards.n: Trap: forgetting to convert Celsius to kelvin is the single most common gas-law error on the exam.

cards.q: State Dalton's law of partial pressures.
cards.a: The total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases: P_total = P_A + P_B + P_C + ... Each gas behaves as if it alone occupied the container.

cards.q: Define mole fraction and relate it to partial pressure.
cards.a: Mole fraction X_A = (moles of A) / (total moles of all gases). Partial pressure is P_A = X_A · P_total. Mole fractions are unitless and sum to 1.

cards.q: Apply the correction needed when a gas is collected over water.
cards.a: The collected sample is a mixture of the gas and water vapor, so subtract the vapor pressure of water at that temperature: P_gas = P_total - P_H2O. Only then use PV = nRT for the dry gas.
cards.n: Classic lab-based FRQ trap: forgetting this makes the calculated moles of gas too large.

cards.q: State the postulates of kinetic molecular theory for an ideal gas.
cards.a: 1) Particle volume is negligible compared with container volume. 2) Particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion. 3) Collisions are perfectly elastic (no net KE loss). 4) There are no intermolecular attractions or repulsions. 5) Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.

cards.q: Explain the origin of gas pressure in terms of kinetic molecular theory.
cards.a: Pressure results from the force of countless elastic collisions of gas particles with the container walls per unit area. More particles, higher temperature (faster collisions), or a smaller volume all increase the collision rate and therefore the pressure.

cards.q: State how average kinetic energy of gas particles depends on the gas identity and temperature.
cards.a: Average kinetic energy depends ONLY on absolute temperature: KE_avg = (3/2)kT. At the same temperature, all gases - regardless of molar mass - have the same average kinetic energy.
cards.h: → what it depends on and what it does not
cards.n: Extremely common trap: same temperature means same average KE but NOT the same average speed.

cards.q: Explain how a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution changes when temperature increases.
cards.a: The curve flattens and broadens, its peak shifts to higher speed, and the peak height drops. The total area under the curve is unchanged because the number of particles is constant.
cards.h: → three changes to the curve shape

cards.q: Contrast the Maxwell-Boltzmann curves of two gases with different molar masses at the same temperature.
cards.a: The lighter gas has a broader curve shifted to higher speeds with a lower peak; the heavier gas has a narrower, taller curve peaked at a lower speed. Both distributions correspond to the same average kinetic energy.
cards.h: → which curve is where + shared quantity

cards.q: State the equation for root-mean-square speed of a gas.
cards.a: $u_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$, where M is molar mass in kg/mol, T is in kelvin, and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
cards.h: → one equation with a square root
cards.n: Trap: molar mass must be in kg/mol, not g/mol, when R is in joules.

cards.q: Predict the relative average speeds of He and O₂ at the same temperature.
cards.a: Speed varies as 1/√M, so He (4.0 g/mol) moves faster than O₂ (32.0 g/mol) by a factor of √(32/4) = √8 ≈ 2.8.

cards.q: Explain the two conditions under which a real gas deviates most from ideal behavior.
cards.a: High pressure (particles are crowded, so their own volume is no longer negligible) and low temperature (particles move slowly enough for intermolecular attractions to matter). Ideal behavior is approached at low pressure and high temperature.
cards.h: → two conditions, each with a cause

cards.q: Explain the effect of intermolecular attractions on the measured pressure of a real gas.
cards.a: Attractions pull a molecule back as it approaches the wall, softening the collision, so the measured pressure is LOWER than the ideal gas law predicts. This effect dominates at low temperature and moderate pressure.

cards.q: Explain the effect of finite particle volume on a real gas at very high pressure.
cards.a: The particles themselves occupy a significant fraction of the container, so the free volume available is less than the measured volume. This makes the observed PV/nRT rise above 1 at very high pressure.

cards.q: Identify which gases deviate most from ideal behavior and why.
cards.a: Large gases with many electrons and gases with strong IMFs (especially hydrogen bonding, such as H₂O and NH₃) deviate most. He and H₂, being small with very weak LDFs, behave most ideally.

cards.q: Define molarity and give its equation.
cards.a: Molarity M is the concentration of a solution in moles of solute per liter of SOLUTION: M = mol solute / L solution. Units are mol/L, often written M.
cards.n: Trap: the volume is the final solution volume, not the volume of solvent added.

cards.q: Apply the dilution equation and state what it assumes.
cards.a: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, where subscript 1 is the concentrated stock and 2 is the diluted solution. It works because adding solvent changes the volume but not the moles of solute.

cards.q: Compute the concentration of each ion in 0.20 M CaCl₂.
cards.a: CaCl₂ dissociates into Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻, so [Ca²⁺] = 0.20 M and [Cl⁻] = 0.40 M.
cards.n: Frequent MC trap: forgetting the stoichiometric coefficient doubles or triples an ion's concentration.

cards.q: State how to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.250 M NaCl from solid.
cards.a: Moles needed = 0.250 mol/L x 0.5000 L = 0.125 mol; mass = 0.125 x 58.44 = 7.31 g. Dissolve that mass in a small amount of water in a 500.0 mL volumetric flask, then add water to the calibration mark.

cards.q: Explain what a correct particulate diagram of aqueous NaCl must show.
cards.a: Separate, fully dissociated Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (no NaCl units), each surrounded by water molecules oriented by ion-dipole forces: oxygen ends toward Na⁺ and hydrogen ends toward Cl⁻. The ratio of ions must match the formula.

cards.q: Contrast the particulate representations of a strong electrolyte and a nonelectrolyte in water.
cards.a: A strong electrolyte is drawn as fully separated ions with no intact formula units. A nonelectrolyte such as glucose or ethanol is drawn as intact neutral molecules dispersed among the water molecules.

cards.q: Define the retention factor (R_f) in paper or thin-layer chromatography.
cards.a: $R_f = \frac{d_{spot}}{d_{solvent}}$, the distance the component traveled divided by the distance the solvent front traveled from the same origin. R_f is always between 0 and 1.

cards.q: Predict which component travels farthest on a polar stationary phase with a nonpolar mobile phase.
cards.a: The least polar component travels farthest, because it interacts weakly with the polar stationary phase and is carried along by the nonpolar solvent. Polar components adsorb strongly and stay near the origin.
cards.n: The answer reverses if you swap the phase polarities, so always state which phase is polar in your justification.

cards.q: Decide which separation technique to use for: sand in water, salt in water, and two miscible liquids.
cards.a: Sand in water: filtration (insoluble solid, size difference). Salt in water: evaporation or distillation (large boiling-point difference). Two miscible liquids: fractional distillation (different IMF strengths, so different boiling points).
cards.h: → three techniques matched to three mixtures

cards.q: State the 'like dissolves like' rule and explain it energetically.
cards.a: A solute dissolves in a solvent when solute-solvent interactions are comparable in type and strength to the solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions being disrupted. Polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents; nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents.

cards.q: Predict the solubility of NaCl, I₂, and CH₃OH in water versus in hexane.
cards.a: NaCl dissolves in water (ion-dipole) but not hexane. I₂ dissolves in hexane (LDF-LDF) but barely in water. CH₃OH dissolves in water because it hydrogen bonds, and only slightly in hexane.

cards.q: Explain why the water solubility of straight-chain alcohols falls as the carbon chain lengthens.
cards.a: Only the -OH group can hydrogen bond with water; the growing hydrocarbon chain is nonpolar and cannot. As the nonpolar fraction of the molecule grows, it increasingly dominates and solubility drops.
cards.n: This 'polar head, nonpolar tail' reasoning is also the AP answer for soaps and for why CH₃OH is miscible but C₈H₁₇OH is not.

cards.q: Explain the three energy steps involved in forming a solution.
cards.a: 1) Separate solute particles (endothermic). 2) Separate solvent particles to make room (endothermic). 3) Form solute-solvent interactions (exothermic). The sign of the overall enthalpy of solution is the sum of these three.

cards.q: Define saturated, unsaturated, and supersaturated solutions.
cards.a: Unsaturated: less solute is dissolved than the maximum, so more can dissolve. Saturated: dissolved solute is in dynamic equilibrium with undissolved solid at the maximum concentration. Supersaturated: more solute is dissolved than the equilibrium amount; it is unstable and crystallizes when disturbed.

cards.q: Recall the solubility rules for compounds that are generally SOLUBLE in water.
cards.a: Soluble: all Group 1 (alkali metal) and ammonium (NH₄⁺) salts; all nitrates (NO₃⁻), acetates, chlorates, and perchlorates; halides EXCEPT those of Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, and Hg₂²⁺; sulfates EXCEPT those of Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, and Ag⁺.
cards.n: Group 1, NH₄⁺, and NO₃⁻ have NO exceptions - lean on those three when predicting a precipitate.

cards.q: Recall the solubility rules for compounds that are generally INSOLUBLE in water.
cards.a: Insoluble: carbonates (CO₃²⁻), phosphates (PO₄³⁻), chromates, sulfides (S²⁻), and hydroxides (OH⁻) - except when paired with Group 1 cations or NH₄⁺. Ba(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, and Ca(OH)₂ are moderately soluble.

cards.q: Identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing photon energy.
cards.a: Radio < microwave < infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-ray < gamma. Energy increases as wavelength decreases.

cards.q: Identify the molecular transition probed by microwave, infrared, and UV-visible radiation.
cards.a: Microwave excites molecular ROTATION; infrared excites bond VIBRATION (stretching and bending); ultraviolet-visible excites ELECTRONIC transitions between energy levels. Higher-energy photons drive larger energy-gap processes.
cards.h: → three regions matched to three motions
cards.n: AP asks this as 'which region would you use to identify the bonds present?' - the answer is IR.

cards.q: State the two equations relating photon energy, frequency, and wavelength.
cards.a: E = hν and c = λν, so E = hc/λ. Here h = 6.626 x 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 x 10⁸ m/s.
cards.n: Trap: wavelength must be in meters before using c = λν; nm values must be multiplied by 10⁻⁹.

cards.q: Explain the relationship between a photon's wavelength and its energy.
cards.a: They are inversely proportional: E = hc/λ, so shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher energy per photon. Gamma rays carry far more energy per photon than radio waves.

cards.q: Explain the photoelectric effect and the role of the threshold frequency.
cards.a: Light striking a metal ejects electrons only if each photon's energy hν meets or exceeds the metal's work function (threshold frequency). Below that threshold no electrons are emitted no matter how intense or how long the light is applied.

cards.q: Compute the kinetic energy of an electron ejected in the photoelectric effect.
cards.a: KE = hν - φ, where φ is the work function (the minimum energy to remove the electron). Any photon energy beyond the threshold becomes kinetic energy of the ejected electron.

cards.q: Explain why increasing light intensity below the threshold frequency ejects no electrons.
cards.a: Each electron absorbs one photon, so what matters is the energy PER photon, not the total energy delivered. More intense light sends more photons, but if each is too weak the electron cannot be freed - evidence that light is quantized.
cards.n: This is the classic AP argument that light is particulate; a wave model would predict that any intensity eventually works.

cards.q: State the Beer-Lambert law and define each term.
cards.a: A = εbc, where A is absorbance (unitless), ε is molar absorptivity (a constant for a given species at a given wavelength), b is the path length of the cell, and c is molar concentration. Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration.

cards.q: Apply a Beer-Lambert calibration curve to find an unknown concentration.
cards.a: Measure absorbance of standards of known concentration at a fixed wavelength, plot A versus c, and fit a straight line through the origin. Read the unknown's concentration from its measured absorbance, or divide A by the slope (εb).
cards.h: → plotting procedure + how to read it

cards.q: Explain why absorbance is measured at the wavelength of maximum absorbance.
cards.a: At λ_max the absorbance changes most per unit concentration, giving the greatest sensitivity and the smallest relative error, and the reading is least affected by small errors in wavelength setting.

cards.q: Predict what happens to absorbance when a colored solution is diluted by half.
cards.a: Absorbance is halved, because A is directly proportional to concentration at constant path length and wavelength. Percent transmittance, however, does not double - it is logarithmically related to A.

cards.q: Contrast a physical change with a chemical change at the particulate level.
cards.a: Physical change: only the attractions between particles are disrupted; the particles themselves are unchanged (melting, boiling, dissolving). Chemical change: bonds within particles break and new bonds form, so different substances exist afterward.
cards.n: Dissolving NaCl in water is classified as a physical change on the AP exam even though the ions separate.

cards.q: Identify the macroscopic evidence that a chemical change has occurred.
cards.a: Gas evolved that is not simply boiling, a precipitate forming, a permanent color change, a temperature change with no external heating, light emitted, or a new odor. Confirmation requires showing a new substance is present.
cards.n: Bubbles alone can mean boiling; AP wants evidence tied to the formation of a new substance.

cards.q: Explain why dissolving an ionic solid in water is treated as a physical change.
cards.a: Water molecules pull the ions apart by ion-dipole attraction. The ions are chemically unchanged and can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the water, so only interparticle attractions were disrupted.

cards.q: Define a net ionic equation.
cards.a: An equation showing only the species that actually change: soluble strong electrolytes are written as separated aqueous ions and all spectator ions are cancelled. Both mass and total charge must balance.
cards.h: → what is kept, what is cancelled
cards.n: Charge balance is scored separately; a net ionic equation with unbalanced charge earns no credit.

cards.q: Define a spectator ion.
cards.a: An ion that is present in the same aqueous, unchanged form both before and after the reaction, so it cancels out of the complete ionic equation and does not appear in the net ionic equation.

cards.q: State which species are written as separated ions and which are kept as complete formulas in an ionic equation.
cards.a: Separate: strong acids, strong bases, and soluble ionic salts labeled (aq). Keep intact: all solids (s), liquids (l), gases (g), weak acids, weak bases, and molecular compounds such as water.
cards.n: Writing a weak acid such as CH3COOH as separated ions is one of the most common AP scoring errors.

cards.q: Write the net ionic equation for aqueous silver nitrate mixed with aqueous sodium chloride.
cards.a: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Sodium ion and nitrate ion are spectators and are omitted.

cards.q: State the solubility guidelines most often required on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Always soluble: Group 1 cations, NH4⁺, NO3⁻, ClO4⁻, and most acetates. Generally insoluble: most carbonates, phosphates, sulfides, and hydroxides, plus the halides of Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, and Hg2²⁺.
cards.n: No solubility table is provided on the exam, so the always-soluble rules must be memorized.

cards.q: Explain what makes a solute a strong electrolyte and why that matters for ionic equations.
cards.a: A strong electrolyte dissociates essentially completely into free ions in water (strong acids, strong bases, soluble salts). Because it truly exists as separate ions in solution, it is written in separated ionic form.

cards.q: Explain what a particulate diagram drawn after a precipitation reaction must show.
cards.a: The precipitate drawn as a neutral cluster of alternating cations and anions, the spectator ions still drawn as separate hydrated ions in correct relative numbers, and any leftover excess reactant ions still in solution.
cards.n: Students routinely forget to draw the excess reactant ions that survive after the limiting reactant is used up.

cards.q: State the relationship used to convert between mass and moles of a substance.
cards.a: n = m / M, where n is moles, m is mass in grams, and M is molar mass in g/mol. Mole ratios taken from the balanced equation then connect moles of one species to moles of another.

cards.q: Explain why the coefficients of a balanced equation give mole ratios rather than mass ratios.
cards.a: Coefficients count particles, and a mole is a fixed number of particles. Masses of equal particle counts differ because molar masses differ, so masses must be converted to moles before the ratio is applied.

cards.q: Define the limiting reactant and state how to identify it.
cards.a: The reactant consumed completely first, which sets the maximum amount of product. Identify it by dividing the moles of each reactant by its coefficient in the balanced equation; the smallest quotient is the limiting reactant.
cards.n: Compare moles divided by coefficients, never raw masses and never raw moles.

cards.q: State how to find the amount of excess reactant remaining after a reaction goes to completion.
cards.a: Remaining moles = initial moles of the excess reactant minus the moles consumed, where moles consumed = moles of limiting reactant times the coefficient ratio. Multiply by molar mass if grams are requested.

cards.q: Define theoretical yield, actual yield, and percent yield.
cards.a: Theoretical yield is the maximum product predicted from the limiting reactant. Actual yield is the mass really recovered. Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%.

cards.q: Explain why an experimental percent yield is usually below 100%.
cards.a: The reaction may be incomplete or reversible, competing side reactions may consume reactant, product is lost during transfer and filtration, and some product may stay dissolved in the solvent.
cards.n: A percent yield above 100% indicates impure or incompletely dried product, not a better reaction.

cards.q: State the definition of molarity and its equation.
cards.a: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution: M = mol solute / L solution, with units mol/L.
cards.n: The volume is liters of final solution, not liters of solvent added.

cards.q: State the dilution relationship and the reason it works.
cards.a: M1V1 = M2V2. Adding solvent does not change the moles of solute, so concentration falls in exact proportion to the increase in solution volume.

cards.q: Determine the concentration of sulfate ion in 0.10 M Al2(SO4)3.
cards.a: 0.30 M. Each formula unit releases three SO4²⁻ ions, so [SO4²⁻] = 3 x 0.10 M. The aluminum ion concentration is 0.20 M.
cards.n: Forgetting to multiply by the ion subscript is a classic concentration trap.

cards.q: State the full sequence of steps for a mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem with a limiting reactant.
cards.a: Balance the equation; convert each reactant mass to moles; divide each by its coefficient and take the smallest to find the limiting reactant; use the mole ratio to get moles of product; multiply by the molar mass of the product.

cards.q: Define a titration.
cards.a: A procedure in which a solution of accurately known concentration (the titrant) is delivered from a burette into a measured volume of analyte until the reaction is exactly complete, allowing the unknown concentration to be calculated.

cards.q: Contrast the equivalence point with the endpoint of a titration.
cards.a: The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point at which moles of titrant exactly satisfy the balanced equation. The endpoint is the observed indicator color change used to approximate it; the gap between them is titration error.
cards.n: These are not synonyms; free response questions often ask which one the indicator actually signals.

cards.q: State the general procedure for finding an unknown concentration from titration data.
cards.a: Compute moles of titrant as M x V; convert to moles of analyte using the mole ratio from the balanced equation; divide by the analyte volume in liters to get its molarity.
cards.n: MaVa = MbVb is valid only for a 1:1 mole ratio; otherwise the coefficients must be included.

cards.q: Explain the effect on the calculated result of rinsing a burette with distilled water instead of with titrant.
cards.a: The titrant in the burette is diluted, so a larger volume is delivered before the endpoint. The calculated moles of titrant, and therefore the reported analyte concentration, come out too high.
cards.n: Rinsing the receiving flask with water is harmless because the moles of analyte in it are unchanged.

cards.q: Define a primary standard and explain what standardizing a solution means.
cards.a: A primary standard is a pure, stable, accurately weighable solid used to prepare a solution of exactly known concentration. Standardizing means titrating another solution against it to determine that solution's true concentration.

cards.q: Decide how to choose an appropriate indicator for an acid-base titration.
cards.a: Choose an indicator whose color-change range brackets the pH at the equivalence point: phenolphthalein for a weak acid titrated with strong base or for strong-strong, methyl orange for a weak base titrated with strong acid.

cards.q: Define gravimetric analysis.
cards.a: A quantitative technique in which an excess of a precipitating reagent removes the target ion as an insoluble solid; the precipitate is filtered, dried, and weighed, and its mass is converted to moles of the target ion in the original sample.
cards.n: The precipitating reagent must be in excess so that essentially all of the target ion is captured.

cards.q: Explain why a gravimetric precipitate must be washed and dried to constant mass.
cards.a: Washing removes soluble spectator ions clinging to the crystals and drying removes residual water. Both would otherwise add mass, making the calculated amount of analyte too large.

cards.q: Identify the three broad categories of chemical reaction emphasized in AP Chemistry.
cards.a: Acid-base reactions (proton transfer), precipitation reactions (formation of an insoluble ionic solid), and oxidation-reduction reactions (electron transfer).
cards.h: → three names with the transferred species

cards.q: Define a precipitation reaction and illustrate its net ionic form.
cards.a: Two soluble ionic solutions are mixed and oppositely charged ions combine into an insoluble solid. Example: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s).

cards.q: Predict whether mixing aqueous sodium sulfate with aqueous barium nitrate gives a precipitate, and write the net ionic equation.
cards.a: Yes, barium sulfate precipitates: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s). Sodium ion and nitrate ion are spectators.

cards.q: Define a Bronsted-Lowry acid and a Bronsted-Lowry base.
cards.a: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Every such reaction transfers H⁺ from the acid to the base, producing a conjugate base and a conjugate acid.

cards.q: State the net ionic equation for the neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base.
cards.a: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l), equivalently H3O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2 H2O(l).
cards.n: If either the acid or the base is weak, the weak species stays intact in the net ionic equation.

cards.q: Predict the products formed when a strong acid is added to a metal carbonate.
cards.a: Carbon dioxide gas, water, and the dissolved salt. For an insoluble carbonate: CaCO3(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g).
cards.n: Carbonic acid is unstable and decomposes, so H2CO3 should not be left as a final product.

cards.q: Define a combustion reaction and state the products of complete hydrocarbon combustion.
cards.a: A rapid exothermic reaction with O2. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon yields CO2 and H2O; incomplete combustion with limited oxygen yields CO or soot as well.

cards.q: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons and oxidation numbers.
cards.a: Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation number; reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation number. The two always occur together (LEO says GER).

cards.q: State the rules for assigning oxidation numbers.
cards.a: Free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge; the sum is 0 for a neutral compound and equals the charge for a polyatomic ion; Group 1 = +1, Group 2 = +2, F = -1; H = +1 except -1 with metals; O = -2 except -1 in peroxides and +2 in OF2.
cards.n: The rules apply in priority order, so fluorine and Groups 1 and 2 outrank the hydrogen and oxygen rules.

cards.q: Determine the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, Cr2O7²⁻.
cards.a: +6. The seven oxygens contribute 7(-2) = -14, and the total must equal -2, so 2x - 14 = -2 and x = +6.

cards.q: Identify how to tell the oxidizing agent from the reducing agent in a redox reaction.
cards.a: The oxidizing agent is the species that is reduced: it gains electrons and its oxidation number decreases. The reducing agent is the species that is oxidized: it loses electrons and its oxidation number increases.
cards.n: The labels run opposite to intuition; each agent undergoes the process named after the other.

cards.q: Decide quickly whether a given reaction is an oxidation-reduction reaction.
cards.a: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom on both sides; if any element changes oxidation number, the reaction is redox. Reactions involving a free element on one side are almost always redox.
cards.n: Double-replacement precipitations and acid-base neutralizations are never redox reactions.

cards.q: Define disproportionation.
cards.a: A redox reaction in which one element in a single oxidation state is simultaneously oxidized and reduced, ending up in both a higher and a lower oxidation state.

cards.q: State the half-reaction method for balancing a redox equation in acidic solution.
cards.a: Split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions; balance all elements except O and H; add H2O to balance oxygen; add H⁺ to balance hydrogen; add electrons to balance charge; scale the halves so electrons cancel; add them together.
cards.n: Balance oxygen with water first and only then hydrogen with H⁺; the reverse order does not work.

cards.q: State the extra step needed to balance a redox equation in basic solution.
cards.a: Balance the equation first as if it were acidic, then add to both sides as many OH⁻ as there are H⁺. Combine H⁺ + OH⁻ into H2O on that side and cancel any water appearing on both sides.

cards.q: Balance in acidic solution: MnO4⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺.
cards.a: MnO4⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H2O + 5 Fe³⁺. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons, so five Fe²⁺ are oxidized.

cards.q: Explain the two quantities that must be conserved in a balanced redox equation.
cards.a: Mass, meaning the atoms of every element match on both sides, and charge, meaning the total charge on the left equals the total charge on the right. Equivalently, electrons lost must equal electrons gained.

cards.q: Define the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.a: The change in the concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, usually in mol/(L·s). It is reported as a positive number, so reactant concentration changes carry a negative sign in the definition.

cards.q: State how the rates of the individual species relate for the reaction aA + bB → cC + dD.
cards.a: rate = -(1/a)Δ[A]/Δt = -(1/b)Δ[B]/Δt = (1/c)Δ[C]/Δt = (1/d)Δ[D]/Δt. Dividing by each coefficient produces a single rate value for the whole reaction.
cards.n: Species with larger coefficients change concentration faster, not slower.

cards.q: For 2 N2O5 → 4 NO2 + O2, oxygen appears at 0.020 M/s. Determine the rate at which N2O5 disappears.
cards.a: 0.040 M/s. The stoichiometric ratio of N2O5 to O2 is 2 to 1, so -Δ[N2O5]/Δt = 2 x 0.020 M/s.

cards.q: Explain why the rate of most reactions decreases as the reaction proceeds.
cards.a: Reactant concentrations fall as they are consumed, so productive collisions become less frequent. Because rate depends on concentration through the rate law, the instantaneous rate declines toward zero.

cards.q: Identify the factors that change the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.a: Concentration or partial pressure of reactants, temperature, surface area of any solid reactant, the physical state and degree of mixing, and the presence of a catalyst.
cards.n: A catalyst changes the rate but never changes ΔH, ΔG, or the position of equilibrium.

cards.q: Explain why increasing the surface area of a solid reactant speeds up a reaction.
cards.a: Reaction can occur only where particles meet the exposed surface. Grinding the solid into powder exposes far more particles at once, raising the number of collisions per second without changing any concentration.

cards.q: Explain why a modest increase in temperature produces a large increase in reaction rate.
cards.a: Higher temperature shifts the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution toward higher energies, so a much larger fraction of collisions carry at least the activation energy. Collision frequency rises slightly too, but the exponential energy factor dominates.

cards.q: Define a rate law.
cards.a: An experimentally determined equation expressing rate in terms of reactant concentrations, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are the reaction orders and k is the temperature-dependent rate constant.

cards.q: Define reaction order and overall reaction order.
cards.a: The order with respect to a species is the exponent on that species concentration in the rate law. The overall order is the sum of all the exponents. Orders are usually 0, 1, or 2 but may be fractional.

cards.q: Explain why the exponents in a rate law cannot be read from the balanced overall equation.
cards.a: The rate law reflects only the rate-determining elementary step, not the overall stoichiometry. Orders must be measured experimentally or derived from a proposed mechanism; only a single elementary step may use its own coefficients.
cards.n: Copying the balanced coefficients into the rate law is among the most heavily penalized AP errors.

cards.q: State the units of the rate constant k for zero-, first-, and second-order reactions.
cards.a: Zero order: M/s. First order: s⁻¹. Second order: M⁻¹s⁻¹. In general the units are M^(1-n)·s⁻¹ for an overall order n.
cards.n: The units of k by themselves can reveal the overall order on a multiple-choice question.

cards.q: State how to determine reaction orders from a table of initial-rate data.
cards.a: Compare two trials in which only one reactant concentration changes. If that concentration is multiplied by f and the rate is multiplied by f raised to m, the order in that reactant is m. Repeat for each reactant, then substitute one trial to find k.
cards.n: Only vary one concentration at a time; choosing trials where two concentrations change gives a wrong order.

cards.q: Determine the order in A when doubling [A] at constant [B] multiplies the rate by four.
cards.a: Second order in A, because 2 raised to m equals 4 requires m = 2.

cards.q: State the integrated rate law for a zero-order reaction and the plot that is linear.
cards.a: $[A]_{t} - [A]_{0} = -kt$. A plot of [A] versus time is a straight line with slope -k and intercept [A]0.

cards.q: State the integrated rate law for a first-order reaction and the plot that is linear.
cards.a: $\ln [A]_{t} - \ln [A]_{0} = -kt$. A plot of ln[A] versus time is a straight line with slope -k.

cards.q: State the integrated rate law for a second-order reaction and the plot that is linear.
cards.a: $\frac{1}{[A]_{t}} - \frac{1}{[A]_{0}} = kt$. A plot of 1/[A] versus time is a straight line with slope +k.
cards.n: The second-order slope is positive, while the zero- and first-order slopes are negative.

cards.q: Identify the reaction order from which concentration-versus-time plot comes out linear.
cards.a: A straight line for [A] vs t means zero order; for ln[A] vs t means first order; for 1/[A] vs t means second order. The order is whichever transformation linearizes the data.
cards.n: AP frequently supplies all three plots and asks which one is straight.

cards.q: Define half-life and give the half-life expression for a first-order reaction.
cards.a: The half-life is the time for the reactant concentration to fall to half its current value. For a first-order reaction $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$, which is independent of the starting concentration.

cards.q: Explain why a constant half-life identifies a reaction as first order.
cards.a: Only for first order does the half-life expression contain no concentration term. Zero-order half-lives grow shorter as the reaction proceeds and second-order half-lives grow longer, so equal successive half-lives means first order.

cards.q: Determine the fraction of a first-order reactant remaining after n half-lives.
cards.a: (1/2) raised to the n. After three half-lives 12.5% remains; after four, 6.25%.

cards.q: Define the collision model of reaction rates.
cards.a: Reactant particles must physically collide to react. The rate equals the collision frequency multiplied by the fraction of collisions that are effective, and only collisions with sufficient energy and correct orientation produce product.

cards.q: State the two requirements for a collision to result in reaction.
cards.a: The colliding particles must have combined kinetic energy at least equal to the activation energy, and they must be oriented so that the atoms that need to bond actually meet.

cards.q: Define activation energy.
cards.a: The minimum energy colliding particles must possess to reach the transition state and go on to products. On an energy profile it is the vertical rise from the reactants to the peak.

cards.q: Define the activated complex and distinguish it from an intermediate.
cards.a: The activated complex, or transition state, is the highest-energy arrangement at the peak of the profile with old bonds partly broken and new bonds partly formed. It cannot be isolated, whereas an intermediate sits in an energy minimum and can be.

cards.q: State the Arrhenius equation and identify each symbol.
cards.a: $k = A e^{-E_{a}/(RT)}$, where A is the frequency factor including collision orientation, Ea is the activation energy, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), and T is the absolute temperature.
cards.n: Ea must be expressed in joules per mole when R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is used.

cards.q: State the linear form of the Arrhenius equation and how activation energy is extracted from it.
cards.a: $\ln k = -\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \ln A$. A plot of ln k versus 1/T is a straight line of slope -Ea/R with intercept ln A, so Ea = -R times the slope.

cards.q: A plot of ln k versus 1/T has slope -1.2 x 10⁴ K. Determine the activation energy.
cards.a: Ea = -R x slope = -(8.314)(-1.2 x 10⁴) = 1.0 x 10⁵ J/mol, about 1.0 x 10² kJ/mol.
cards.n: A negative slope must yield a positive Ea; a negative activation energy signals a dropped sign.

cards.q: Explain how a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows the effect of temperature on rate.
cards.a: The curve plots the number of particles against kinetic energy. Raising the temperature lowers and broadens the peak and shifts it right, greatly increasing the area beyond Ea, which is the fraction of particles able to react.

cards.q: Explain how adding a catalyst is represented on a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
cards.a: The distribution curve itself is unchanged; the vertical Ea line moves to the left to a lower value, so a larger area under the curve, meaning a larger fraction of particles, now exceeds it.
cards.h: → what moves and what does not
cards.n: A catalyst does not give particles more energy; it lowers the energy bar they must clear.

cards.q: Define a reaction mechanism.
cards.a: The sequence of elementary steps by which reactants are converted to products. The steps must sum to the overall balanced equation and must predict the experimentally observed rate law.

cards.q: Define an elementary step and state how its rate law is written.
cards.a: An elementary step is a single molecular event that occurs exactly as written. Its rate law follows directly from its own coefficients, so A + B → products gives rate = k[A][B] and 2A → products gives rate = k[A]².
cards.n: Only for elementary steps may exponents be taken from coefficients.

cards.q: Define molecularity and name its three types.
cards.a: Molecularity is the number of particles that collide in an elementary step. Unimolecular involves one particle, bimolecular two, and termolecular three; termolecular steps are rare because simultaneous three-body collisions are very unlikely.

cards.q: Define a reaction intermediate.
cards.a: A species produced in one elementary step and consumed in a later step, so it cancels and does not appear in the overall balanced equation. Unlike a transition state it occupies an energy minimum and can sometimes be detected.
cards.n: An intermediate may never appear in a final rate law; it must be substituted away.

cards.q: Define the rate-determining step.
cards.a: The slowest elementary step in a mechanism. It acts as a bottleneck, so the observed rate law matches the rate law of that step once any intermediate has been eliminated.

cards.q: State the predicted rate law when the first elementary step of a mechanism is the slow step.
cards.a: The overall rate law is simply the rate law of that first step, written from its molecularity, because every later step is fast. For a slow A + B → C, the rate law is rate = k[A][B].

cards.q: Explain how to derive the rate law when a fast reversible step precedes the rate-determining step.
cards.a: Write the rate law of the slow step, then eliminate the intermediate: set the forward and reverse rates of the fast equilibrium equal, solve for the intermediate concentration in terms of reactants, and substitute. The constants merge into one observed k.
cards.h: → set forward equal to reverse, then substitute
cards.n: The final rate law must contain only reactants, or a catalyst, and never an intermediate.

cards.q: Explain why an intermediate cannot appear in an experimentally determined rate law.
cards.a: Rate laws are found by varying measurable initial concentrations, but an intermediate is absent at the start and cannot be controlled by the experimenter, so its concentration must be re-expressed in terms of reactants.

cards.q: State the two criteria a proposed mechanism must satisfy to be acceptable.
cards.a: The elementary steps must add up to the overall balanced equation with all intermediates cancelling, and the mechanism must predict the rate law that is observed experimentally.

cards.q: Define a catalyst.
cards.a: A substance that increases reaction rate by providing an alternative mechanism with a lower activation energy. It is consumed in an early step and regenerated in a later step, so it is not used up overall and does not appear in the balanced equation.

cards.q: State what a catalyst does change and what it does not change.
cards.a: Changes: the mechanism, the activation energy (lowered for forward and reverse alike), the rate constant, and the rate. Does not change: ΔH, ΔE, ΔG, the equilibrium constant, the equilibrium position, or the final amount of product.
cards.n: A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but is not shifted.

cards.q: Contrast a homogeneous catalyst with a heterogeneous catalyst.
cards.a: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants, such as aqueous acid catalyzing a reaction in solution. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, typically a solid surface on which gaseous reactants adsorb, react, and desorb.

cards.q: Explain how an enzyme catalyzes a biological reaction.
cards.a: The substrate binds in the enzyme's active site, which holds it in a favorable orientation and stabilizes the transition state, lowering the activation energy. The enzyme is released unchanged and is highly specific to its substrate.

cards.q: Identify the forward activation energy, reverse activation energy, and ΔH on a reaction energy profile.
cards.a: Ea forward is the peak height measured up from the reactants; Ea reverse is the peak height measured up from the products; ΔH is the product energy minus the reactant energy. Therefore ΔH = Ea(forward) - Ea(reverse).
cards.n: Products lying below reactants means the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.

cards.q: Identify the rate-determining step from a multi-step reaction energy profile.
cards.a: Each hump is one elementary step. The rate-determining step is the one with the largest activation energy, measured as the climb from the valley immediately before it up to its own peak.
cards.n: Use the height of the climb from the preceding valley, not the absolute height of the peak above the axis.

cards.q: Explain what the valleys between peaks on a multi-step energy profile represent.
cards.a: They are reaction intermediates: real species at a local energy minimum that are formed in one elementary step and consumed in the next.

cards.q: Contrast endothermic and exothermic processes.
cards.a: Endothermic: the system absorbs energy, q > 0 and ΔH > 0, products lie above reactants in energy, and the surroundings cool. Exothermic: the system releases energy, q < 0 and ΔH < 0, products lie below reactants, and the surroundings warm.
cards.h: → signs plus temperature of the surroundings

cards.q: Define system and surroundings in a thermochemistry problem.
cards.a: The system is the portion of the universe being studied, normally the reacting chemicals. The surroundings are everything else that can exchange energy with it, including the solvent, the container, and the air.
cards.n: In coffee-cup calorimetry the water is part of the surroundings, not the system.

cards.q: State the sign conventions for q and w for a thermodynamic system.
cards.a: q is positive when heat flows into the system (endothermic) and negative when heat flows out (exothermic). w is positive when work is done on the system, as in compression, and negative when the system expands and does work.

cards.q: State the first law of thermodynamics in equation form.
cards.a: ΔE = q + w: the change in internal energy equals heat added to the system plus work done on it. Because energy is conserved, q_system = -q_surroundings.

cards.q: State the expression for pressure-volume work and explain its sign.
cards.a: w = -PΔV at constant external pressure. When the system expands ΔV is positive, so w is negative, reflecting that the system does work on the surroundings.

cards.q: Explain in terms of bond energies why a reaction is exothermic.
cards.a: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy and forming bonds always releases it. If the bonds formed in the products release more energy than was needed to break the bonds in the reactants, the net energy change is negative.

cards.q: Explain why a beaker feels cold during an endothermic reaction in solution.
cards.a: The system absorbs energy from the solution and container, lowering their temperature. Heat then flows from your hand into the beaker, and the loss of energy from your skin is sensed as cold.

cards.q: Define heat and contrast it with temperature.
cards.a: Heat, q, is energy transferred because of a temperature difference and is measured in joules. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles and does not depend on how much sample is present.
cards.n: A large lukewarm tub of water contains far more thermal energy than a small very hot cup.

cards.q: Define specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, and heat capacity.
cards.a: Specific heat capacity c is the energy to raise 1 gram by 1 K, in J/(g·K). Molar heat capacity uses 1 mole instead. Heat capacity C applies to an entire object and is in J/K.

cards.q: State the equation relating heat transferred to temperature change.
cards.a: q = mcΔT, where m is mass in grams, c is specific heat capacity in J/(g·K), and ΔT = T_final - T_initial. A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so either may be used for ΔT.
cards.n: A negative ΔT produces a negative q, correctly showing that the sample released energy.

cards.q: Determine the heat absorbed when 50.0 g of water is warmed from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C, given c = 4.18 J/(g·K).
Explain what a large specific heat capacity indicates about a substance.
cards.a: A large amount of energy is needed per gram to change its temperature, so it heats and cools slowly. Water's unusually high value of 4.18 J/(g·K) comes from its extensive hydrogen bonding.

cards.q: Predict which of two equal-mass samples absorbing equal heat undergoes the larger temperature change.
cards.a: The sample with the smaller specific heat capacity, because ΔT = q/(mc) is inversely proportional to c.

cards.q: Define calorimetry.
